reasoning: ط is emphatic, so a capital T. Adjective pattern fa3l gives raTb (fem. raTbe), as in 'il-jaww raTb'. The short vowel in the adjective is slightly uncertain.
shu and biddi are the Palestinian markers. ق in a'uul is a glottal stop. The verb plus the preposition l-ak is spoken a'uul-lak with a doubled l. Some speakers may drop the first a.
Past-tense verb of the fa3ila type. Palestinian raises the first vowel (fihim, 'irif), and ق is a glottal stop. 'Disgusted' reads as an adjective, but the entry is a verb meaning 'he got disgusted'.
Everyday Palestinian reassurance meaning 'it'll work out'. Long aa in allaah and long ii in kariim.
Form II passive participle with a doubled l: mkhallal, 'pickled'. Used as a collective noun for pickles (plural mkhallalaat).
Levantine month name. ث is pronounced t in everyday speech (taani). Speech normally has the article, it-taani, though the written form drops it.
Urban Ramallah speech says haad with d. The ظ form (haaTH) is a rural or Bedouin-style variant outside the target variety, so I romanized the urban form.
3inna 'at us/our' is the Palestinian form. 7anafiyye is the usual word for faucet, with taa marbuta read as e after ي. I read the verb as form II (naqqaT, 'to drip'), but form I is possible.
Alif maqsura is a. Intransitive 'it boiled, came to a boil'. The transitive 'he boiled (something)' is ghalla.
Palestinian jooz means 'husband', with long oo. Taa marbuta after م is e. In use it is normally possessive, jooz 3ammti 'my aunt's husband'.
Common oath and intensifier, pronounced wallaah with a doubled l and long aa. It also works as 'really?' or 'wow'.
Plural distant demonstrative 'those' (near form hadool). The long oo and the -aak ending are what I expect, but the exact vowel length is slightly uncertain.
fii 'there is', ق in wa't is a glottal stop, and ba- plus murr is the present tense. 3aleek is the masculine 'on you', with ee.
The English says to a female, so the object suffix is -ik, giving asaa3dik (the masculine would be asaa3dak). khalliini is 'let me'.
Palestinian 3anze, with taa marbuta read as e after ز. Strictly it is a she-goat; the collective 'goats' is ma3z.
Small change, as in 'ma3ak fraaTa?'. Taa marbuta after emphatic ط is a. fakke is also common in Palestinian speech.
Literally 'may He ruin your house'. It expresses exasperation, and can also express grudging admiration. beet has ee, so beetak. The yikhrib versus yikhrab vowel is a small uncertainty.
Religious condolence formula, so ق keeps [q]. Final hamza is written '. Some speakers drop the final hamza (il-baqa lillaah).
Nisba from the plural Sanaayi3 'crafts', so a skilled tradesman. Emphatic ص is S. Known across the Levant, though Palestinians also say mi3allim.
MSA-origin but fully everyday. ظ is an emphatic fricative and the scheme offers TH for it, though it may be realized nearer [zˤ] or [dˤ]. The doubled TH comes from the shadda.
Standard Palestinian reply to 'how are you'. The article elides after the vowel-final maashi: maashi l-7aal.
Allaah plus a subjunctive verb is the usual prayer form. filasTiin is the Palestinian pronunciation, with emphatic ط. ظ is written TH, as in entry 1572.
Media-register word. ذ is likely pronounced d (possibly z) in speech, and taa marbuta after ح is e. majzara is the more common Palestinian word for 'massacre'.
Form II verb dawwar, usually dawwar 3ala 'look for'. Doubled w from the shadda.
Palestinian iid 'hand', also used for the arm. Long ii, not MSA yad.
